patient.title: The School Principal
patient.initialQuote: My chest is tight. But look at your station, Doctor. Disorganized.

fenn.initial: New shift, new patient. Let’s take this one clue at a time.
fenn.labMenuHint: For crushing chest pain with shock, start with the tracing; use troponin to establish injury and the remaining tubes to judge organ perfusion and treatment safety.
fenn.labMenuPatient: Choose the test that changes what you do now, not the one that merely fills another box.
fenn.diagnosisCorrect: Nicely reasoned. We have the diagnosis; now let’s take care of the person attached to it.
fenn.diagnosisWrong: A reasonable attempt. Look once more at II, III, and aVF—the territory is waiting for you.
fenn.diagnosisUnsupported: That diagnosis does not account for crushing chest pain, shock, and a territorial ST-elevation pattern. Start with the tracing.
fenn.differentialLocked: Acute coronary occlusion is a defensible start. Now establish the territory and its haemodynamic consequences.
fenn.debrief: He called it a routine appointment. I suspect his wife will be editing that account rather firmly.

hpi: A 67-year-old retired school principal presents with 45 minutes of central crushing chest pain radiating to the left arm and jaw. He is diaphoretic, progressively dyspnoeic, and insists he drove himself because the appointment was ‘routine.’ He missed his antihypertensive and statin this morning. The pain began at rest and has not improved with position.

chart.PMH: Hypertension; hypercholesterolaemia; no prior cardiac events.
chart.Medications: Amlodipine 5 mg daily; atorvastatin 40 mg daily — both missed today.
chart.Family Hx: Father died of a cardiac event aged 71.
chart.Social Hx: Retired; non-smoker; occasional wine; sedentary; lives with wife.

diagnosticReasoning.earlyRecognitionFeedback: Strong early recognition. The presentation supports acute coronary syndrome, but the ECG is required to identify the ST-elevation pattern and territory.

mustNotMiss.feedback: Reasonable must-not-miss choice: dyspnoea, tachycardia, hypoxaemia, and hypotension can indicate pulmonary embolism.
Reasonable must-not-miss choice: acute dangerous chest pain warrants consideration of aortic dissection before antithrombotic treatment.

reasonableAlternatives.feedback: Pericarditis can cause acute chest pain, although positional or pleuritic pain would support it more strongly.
Reflux can mimic chest discomfort, but radiation, diaphoresis, and haemodynamic instability make it less likely here.
Spontaneous pneumothorax can cause sudden chest pain and dyspnoea, but the examination does not show unilateral breath-sound loss.

finalFeedback.acute-coronary-syndrome-acs: You recognized the correct syndrome, but the ECG now supports a more specific diagnosis: ST-elevation myocardial infarction.
finalFeedback.myocardial-infarction-heart-attack: You recognized myocardial infarction, but the ECG now establishes the ST-elevation subtype. Commit with the available specificity.
finalFeedback.non-st-elevation-myocardial-infarction-n: Acute infarction is directionally correct, but ST elevation in II, III, and aVF rules out NSTEMI.
finalFeedback.pulmonary-embolism-pe: Pulmonary embolism was reasonable to consider initially, but it does not explain the territorial inferior ST elevations with reciprocal changes.
finalFeedback.aortic-dissection: Aortic dissection was reasonable to exclude, but the ECG and absent dissection features now favor acute coronary occlusion.

diagnosticReasoning.correctFeedback: Correct — Inferior STEMI with right-ventricular involvement. Opening management…
diagnosticReasoning.patientCorrect: Inferior myocardial infarction. That is considerably more serious than what I told my wife.
diagnosticReasoning.patientWrong: That answer did not inspire confidence. Perhaps review the tracing before pronouncing me diagnosed.

history.title: ADDITIONAL HISTORY
history.text: He recalls a 10-minute episode of exertional chest pressure two weeks ago that resolved with rest and was dismissed as indigestion. Today’s pain is not pleuritic, positional, or reproducible. No tearing pain to the back, syncope, unilateral leg swelling, recent immobilisation, or prior venous thromboembolism.
history.quote: “I had reports to finish. A man of my standing does not let discomfort derail the curriculum.”
history.fennick: One brief exertional episode two weeks ago. Today’s pain is nonpleuritic, nonpositional, and nonreproducible; no tearing pain or thromboembolic history.
history.hint: Which coronary syndrome can begin with exertional warning pain, then progress to prolonged pressure at rest with diaphoresis and haemodynamic compromise?

exam.title: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
exam.text: Diaphoretic and pale, maintaining an upright posture despite visible discomfort. S4 present. Bilateral basal crackles. JVP mildly elevated. Peripheral pulses weak. Skin cool and clammy. No murmur or peripheral oedema.
exam.quote: “Basic patient care. The crackling in my lungs—I assume that is relevant.”
exam.fennick: Pale and diaphoretic. Cool weak pulses, an S4, basal crackles, and mildly elevated JVP; no murmur or unilateral breath-sound loss.
exam.hint: The cool periphery marks poor forward flow while crackles mark backward congestion. What acute cardiac process can produce both?

imaging.title: CHEST IMAGING
imaging.text: Chest radiograph: mild pulmonary venous congestion. Cardiac silhouette upper-normal. No pneumothorax, focal consolidation, or aortic widening.
imaging.quote: “I attributed that to poor ventilation in my study. I was incorrect.”
imaging.fennick: Mild pulmonary venous congestion. No focal opacity, pneumothorax, or widened mediastinum.
imaging.hint: The film excludes several chest-pain mimics but does not locate a coronary lesion. Which bedside test should do that next?

labs.name: CBC
labs.result: WBC 13.2 (stress leukocytosis). Hgb 14.8. Platelets 290. No major abnormality.
labs.remark: A raised white count? I have not missed a day through illness in thirty-two years.
labs.fennick: Mild leukocytosis; haemoglobin and platelets are preserved.
labs.hint: Nothing here explains the chest pain. Treat the white count as possible physiologic stress and keep looking for the time-critical result.

labs.name: CMP
labs.result: Na 138, K 4.1, creatinine 1.3, glucose 9.2. Mild hypoperfusion pattern.
labs.remark: My kidneys are objecting too? This is becoming an administrative revolt.
labs.fennick: Creatinine and glucose are mildly elevated; potassium is preserved.
labs.hint: These values help with perfusion and medication safety, but they do not identify the cause of the chest pain. What test localizes myocardial ischaemia?

labs.name: EKG
labs.result: Sinus tachycardia. ST elevation in II, III, and aVF with reciprocal ST depression in I and aVL. Right-sided lead V4R also shows ST elevation.
labs.fennick: ST elevation in II, III, and aVF with reciprocal depression in I and aVL; V4R is also elevated.
labs.hint: II, III, and aVF share the inferior wall; reciprocal change strengthens that pattern. What does additional ST elevation in V4R say about ventricular involvement?
labs.remark: That expression suggests the tracing has answered a question I have not.

labs.name: Troponin
labs.result: Troponin I 2.8 ng/mL (normal <0.04), rising on serial measurement: active myocardial injury.
labs.fennick: Troponin is markedly elevated and rising on repeat measurement.
labs.remark: That result has risen again. I gather waiting for another sample will not improve matters.
labs.hint: Troponin proves myocardial injury, but it cannot distinguish STEMI from NSTEMI or identify territory. Which already-available test supplies that information?

labs.name: Lipase
labs.result: Lipase within reference range.
labs.remark: So the abdominal organs are not leading this inquiry. One department has been cleared.
labs.fennick: Lipase is within the reference range.
labs.hint: A normal lipase weakens pancreatitis; it does not explain shock with radiating chest pressure. Return to the cardiovascular evidence.

labs.name: UA
labs.result: Concentrated urine with mild proteinuria; no pyuria or haematuria.
labs.remark: You required urine while my chest is doing this? I hope the relevance becomes apparent.
labs.fennick: Concentrated urine with mild proteinuria; no pyuria or haematuria.
labs.hint: Concentrated urine can follow reduced renal perfusion. Is this the cause of his collapse, or an effect of it?

labs.name: ABG / VBG
labs.result: pH 7.31, pO₂ 68, lactate 3.4, pCO₂ 32: cardiogenic shock physiology.
labs.remark: I feel colder now—and considerably less interested in debating your methods.
labs.fennick: Acidaemia, hypoxaemia, and elevated lactate with a low carbon dioxide.
labs.hint: The gas grades the severity of impaired perfusion; it does not name the cause. Pair it with the blood pressure, lung findings, and ECG.

labs.name: Coags
labs.result: PT/INR 1.1 and PTT 28: normal baseline before anticoagulation.
labs.remark: Normal clotting. Good. I would prefer to keep the blood on the inside.
labs.fennick: Baseline coagulation times are within reference range.
labs.hint: This result matters before antithrombotic or fibrinolytic therapy, but it is a safety check rather than a diagnostic answer.

labs.name: Right-sided ECG leads
labs.result: Right-sided tracing shows 1.5 mm ST elevation in V4R.
labs.remark: Another tracing. Your expression suggests this one changes what you can safely give me.
labs.fennick: V4R shows clear ST elevation.
labs.hint: Right-ventricular infarction is preload dependent. Which familiar anti-ischaemic medication can sharply worsen hypotension here?

management.title: Immediate stabilisation — first actions
management.openingFenn: His pressure is falling and the inferior tracing includes the right ventricle. Stabilize while reperfusion is activated.
management.hint: He is hypotensive and hypoxaemic with a time-critical coronary occlusion. Choose actions that support him and activate definitive reperfusion without reducing preload.
management.hintPatient: If one of those choices lowers my pressure further, I suggest you discard it.
management.prompt: Inferior STEMI with worsening cardiogenic shock: BP 76/44, HR 124, O₂ 90%. What do you do first?
management.promptRemark: Doctor, the pressure is worse. I would appreciate a decision rather than another observation.

staffUpdate.name: Nursing staff
staffUpdate.message: His blood pressure has fallen to 76/44. He is increasingly confused, his oxygen saturation is 90%, and urine output has dropped.

options.text: Give aspirin, begin monitoring, and activate the cath lab immediately
options.feedback: Correct. Give aspirin, support oxygenation when hypoxaemic, establish IV access and continuous monitoring, and activate reperfusion immediately. With right-ventricular involvement and hypotension, avoid nitrates and reassess preload carefully.
options.patientCorrect: Aspirin, lines, monitors. At last—a plan with verbs in it.

options.text: Morphine, oxygen, nitrates, and aspirin—the traditional MONA bundle
options.feedback: Nitrates reduce venous return and can precipitate profound hypotension in preload-dependent right-ventricular infarction. Morphine may also worsen hypotension and delay oral antiplatelet absorption.
options.fennWrong: Nitrates reduce preload; this right ventricle cannot afford that.
options.patientWrong: Everything has tilted. If that was meant to help, it has not.

options.text: One-litre IV fluid bolus before activating the cath lab
options.feedback: A cautious fluid challenge may sometimes support isolated right-ventricular infarction, but a full litre is unsafe with crackles and pulmonary congestion. Reassess in small increments and do not delay reperfusion.
options.fennWrong: The crackles make a blind litre a poor bargain.
options.patientWrong: I can breathe less easily now. Please reconsider whatever is entering that line.

options.text: Urgent echocardiogram before initiating treatment
options.feedback: The ECG already establishes an occlusive infarction requiring immediate treatment. Bedside echocardiography may clarify function or complications, but it must run alongside—not before—reperfusion activation.
options.fennWrong: Echo can answer details while the cath call is already happening.
options.patientWrong: Another examination? Doctor, I am becoming less available for further assessment.

management.quote: “You are being aggressive. Good. Half-measures produce half-results.”
management.fennick: There we are—the ECG gave us the diagnosis. Now we keep him steady while reperfusion catches up.

management.title: Reperfusion strategy
management.openingFenn: The transfer estimate exceeds the PCI window. Choose the reperfusion path that starts before the ambulance leaves.
management.hint: Compare the estimated first-medical-contact-to-device time with the 120-minute threshold. If PCI misses that window and there is no contraindication, another reperfusion route must begin now.
management.hintPatient: The distance will not shorten because we prefer a balloon.
management.prompt: The nearest PCI-capable centre is 140 minutes away. Which reperfusion strategy is appropriate?
management.promptRemark: One hundred and forty minutes? Even my least punctual teachers could improve upon that.

options.text: Transfer for primary PCI without treatment—the balloon is always preferred
options.feedback: Primary PCI is preferred when device treatment can occur within 120 minutes of first medical contact. At 140 minutes, transfer without fibrinolysis leaves viable myocardium untreated for too long.
options.fennWrong: A preferred treatment delivered too late is not the preferred strategy.
options.patientWrong: You intend to place me in an ambulance and simply watch the clock? Unacceptable.

options.text: Administer alteplase now, then transfer for pharmacoinvasive PCI
options.feedback: Correct. If PCI cannot be achieved within 120 minutes and no contraindication exists, give fibrinolysis promptly and transfer for rescue PCI if it fails or routine angiography within 2–24 hours if it succeeds.
options.patientCorrect: Treat the obstruction here, then transfer me. Efficient. Proceed.

options.text: Unfractionated heparin alone
options.feedback: Heparin limits thrombus propagation but does not reliably reopen the occluded artery. It is adjunctive therapy; a reperfusion strategy is still required now.
options.fennWrong: Anticoagulation supports reperfusion; it does not replace it.
options.patientWrong: Preventing matters from worsening is not the same as correcting them, is it?

options.text: Observe serial troponins before committing to reperfusion
options.feedback: ST-elevation infarction is diagnosed from the clinical presentation and ECG. Serial biomarkers help quantify injury later; waiting for them before reperfusion sacrifices myocardium.
options.fennWrong: The artery will not wait for a second biomarker sample.
options.patientWrong: More waiting for another number? I believe my heart has already submitted its report.

management.quote: “The cath lab cannot reach us in time. A logistical failure—but we work with what we have.”
management.fennick: A long journey for a blocked artery. Past 120 minutes, we treat here and transfer.

management.title: Disposition after reperfusion
management.openingFenn: The artery is open, but the first night still carries arrhythmic and mechanical risk.
management.hint: Improved pressure does not erase the first 24–48 hours of arrhythmic and mechanical risk. Choose the unit built for continuous cardiac surveillance.
management.hintPatient: I feel better. I did not say I was ready for my own bed.
management.prompt: Reperfusion succeeds and haemodynamics improve. Where should he go next?
management.promptRemark: The pain is easing. Do not mistake improvement for permission to send me home.

options.text: Admit to coronary care for monitoring and secondary prevention
options.feedback: Correct. Admit to coronary care for continuous rhythm and haemodynamic monitoring, echocardiography, and surveillance for reperfusion arrhythmias or mechanical complications. Begin guideline-directed secondary prevention before discharge.
options.patientCorrect: The cardiac ward. Very well. I expect their monitoring to be punctual.

options.text: General medical ward because the procedure is complete
options.feedback: Recent cardiogenic shock and acute infarction require continuous cardiac and haemodynamic monitoring. A general ward cannot provide the needed surveillance for early arrhythmias or recurrent instability.
options.fennWrong: A routine bed cannot watch a post-shock rhythm continuously.
options.patientWrong: A standard ward after all this? Even I recognize inadequate supervision.

options.text: Discharge home with cardiology follow-up in one week
options.feedback: The first 24–48 hours carry substantial arrhythmic, recurrent-ischaemic, and mechanical risk. Symptom improvement after reperfusion is not evidence that same-day discharge is safe.
options.fennWrong: Reperfusion relieved the pain; it did not erase tonight’s complications.
options.patientWrong: My wife would return me before I reached the driveway—and for once, she would be correct.

options.text: Routine ICU admission despite stable post-reperfusion vitals
options.feedback: General ICU is appropriate when shock persists, ventilation is required, or mechanical circulatory support is needed. With stabilized haemodynamics, a coronary care unit provides the most targeted monitoring.
options.fennWrong: He needs cardiac intensity, not an indiscriminate escalation of location.
options.patientWrong: Intensive care despite improvement? That appears more dramatic than necessary.

management.quote: “The cardiac ward. Understood. I will expect a daily progress report.”
management.fennick: Good. Reperfusion is only the first chapter; the monitor stays close tonight.

hints.fenn: Crushing pain, diaphoresis, and hypotension. I would let the ECG speak next.
hints.patient: A hint? Fine. But I expect the cost to appear in your accounting.

hints.fenn: You’re close. Look at II, III, and aVF—where does that put us?
hints.patient: Your fox appears confident. I hope the confidence is evidence-based.

hints.fenn: V4R is positive. Before reaching for nitrates, consider what his right ventricle is depending on.
hints.patient: If this saves time, I will permit the consultation.

hints.fenn: The balloon is 140 minutes away. Our useful threshold is 120—what can we begin here?
hints.patient: One more clue, then. After that, perhaps treat the patient.

debrief.title: Inferior STEMI with right-ventricular involvement
debrief.pearl: Inferior STEMI is most commonly caused by RCA occlusion. A positive V4R indicates right-ventricular involvement: avoid nitrates and excessive preload reduction. Reperfuse immediately—PCI when achievable within 120 minutes, otherwise fibrinolysis followed by transfer. Post-reperfusion patients require CCU monitoring.

patient.title: The Restaurant Manager's Collapse
patient.initialQuote: Gerald: He was closing up, then he was on the floor. Please—he isn't making sense.

fenn.initial: He cannot give us the story yet. Start with the person who brought him.
fenn.labMenuHint: Check glucose immediately, then electrolytes—especially magnesium—and liver/nutritional markers. The confirmatory vitamin assay is slow and must not hold up treatment.
fenn.labMenuPatient: Gerald: Please order whatever tells you what is dangerous tonight, not next week.
fenn.diagnosisCorrect: Good. Treat the clinical syndrome now; a thiamine level must never hold the door.
fenn.diagnosisWrong: The intoxication history is tempting, but it does not explain the eye findings and ataxia together.
fenn.diagnosisUnsupported: That diagnosis cannot connect malnutrition, confusion, ophthalmoparesis, and ataxia. Build from that neurologic cluster.
fenn.differentialLocked: A nutritional neurologic syndrome is a defensible start. Check glucose, electrolytes, and mimics without delaying treatment.
fenn.debrief: He asked whether breakfast prep was finished before he asked where he was. Some habits survive nearly anything.

hpi: A 54-year-old restaurant owner was found collapsed after closing. His friend reports weeks of poor food intake and daily heavy alcohol use. For roughly two weeks he has misplaced orders and seemed unsteady; three days ago he complained of double vision. Tonight he became confused, could not stand, and stopped speaking coherently.

chart.Collateral Hx: Daily heavy alcohol use; minimal food for several weeks; progressive confusion, diplopia, and gait instability.
chart.Social Hx: Lives alone above his restaurant. Friend Gerald is present and provides collateral history.

diagnosticReasoning.earlyRecognitionFeedback: Strong recognition: malnutrition plus altered mental status, ocular abnormality, and ataxia is enough to treat presumptively.

mustNotMiss.feedback: Must be checked immediately and treated; hypoglycemia can independently cause altered consciousness.
Acute collapse and focal neurologic concerns justify considering intracranial hemorrhage.

reasonableAlternatives.feedback: Plausible from the history, but intoxication alone does not explain the characteristic ocular findings.
Chronic alcohol use and confusion make this reasonable, although the ocular signs and ataxia favor Wernicke encephalopathy.

finalFeedback.alcohol-intoxication: Alcohol intoxication may coexist, but bilateral nystagmus, ophthalmoparesis, ataxia, and malnutrition demand treatment for Wernicke encephalopathy.
finalFeedback.hypoglycemia: Glucose is low and must be corrected, but it does not fully explain the weeks of ataxia and ocular abnormalities.
finalFeedback.hepatic-encephalopathy: There is liver dysfunction, but the ocular motor findings and ataxia make thiamine deficiency the unifying diagnosis.

diagnosticReasoning.correctFeedback: Correct — suspected Wernicke encephalopathy. Treat immediately; do not wait for a thiamine level.
diagnosticReasoning.patientCorrect: Gerald: The vitamin deficiency one? Then give it. Please do not wait for another result.
diagnosticReasoning.patientWrong: Gerald: But what about his eyes? He said he was seeing two of everything three days ago.

history.title: ADDITIONAL HISTORY
history.text: Gerald reports two weeks of confusion and unsteadiness, three days of diplopia, almost no solid food for weeks, and daily heavy alcohol use.
history.quote: Gerald: I thought he was exhausted. I should have noticed sooner.
history.fennick: Two weeks of confusion and gait difficulty, three days of diplopia, minimal food intake, and daily heavy alcohol use.
history.hint: Malnutrition plus confusion, ocular motor findings, and gait dysfunction should trigger treatment for which vitamin-deficiency emergency before confirmation returns?

exam.title: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
exam.text: Confused; GCS 12. Horizontal nystagmus and bilateral abduction weakness. Unable to sit or stand without support. No unilateral weakness. Mild tremor and signs of chronic malnutrition. Airway currently protected.
exam.quote: ...too bright. Turn the kitchen lights down...
exam.fennick: GCS is reduced. Horizontal nystagmus, bilateral abduction weakness, severe truncal and gait instability, tremor, and chronic malnutrition.
exam.hint: The classic triad is often incomplete, but this patient has mental-status change, ophthalmoplegia, and ataxia together. Which diagnosis is treated clinically?

imaging.title: IMAGING
imaging.text: Non-contrast CT head shows no acute hemorrhage, mass, hydrocephalus, or midline shift. Mild generalized volume loss.
imaging.quote: Gerald: The scan is clear, so why can he not sit up?
imaging.fennick: No acute hemorrhage, mass, hydrocephalus, or shift; mild generalized volume loss.
imaging.hint: A normal CT excludes major structural mimics but not a metabolic vitamin-deficiency syndrome. Which diagnosis remains clinical despite unrevealing imaging?

labs.name: Bedside glucose
labs.result: 3.2 mmol/L.
labs.remark: Gerald: His sugar is low. Please correct it while you work out the rest.
labs.fennick: Bedside glucose is below the treatment threshold.
labs.hint: Hypoglycaemia needs immediate dextrose, but it does not explain weeks of ataxia and diplopia. Which co-treatment should precede or accompany glucose here?

labs.name: CBC
labs.result: Hgb 10.8 g/dL, MCV 108 fL, platelets 98 ×10⁹/L: macrocytic anemia and thrombocytopenia.
labs.remark: Gerald: He has barely eaten. I did not know it could affect his blood too.
labs.fennick: Macrocytosis, anaemia, and thrombocytopenia are present.
labs.hint: Macrocytosis supports chronic nutritional and alcohol-related injury, but it does not explain the acute neurologic triad. Keep the syndrome central.

labs.name: CMP + magnesium
labs.result: Na 131, K 3.1, Mg 0.6 mmol/L, albumin 2.6 g/dL.
labs.remark: Gerald: Another critical number. What comes first?
labs.fennick: Potassium and magnesium are low; albumin is reduced.
labs.hint: Magnesium is a cofactor for thiamine-dependent enzymes and its depletion prolongs repolarization. Correct it alongside the suspected deficiency.

labs.name: Liver panel
labs.result: AST 88, ALT 52, GGT 340, bilirubin 2.1: alcohol-associated liver injury pattern.
labs.remark: Gerald: He always said the restaurant drinks were part of the job.
labs.fennick: AST exceeds ALT; GGT and bilirubin are elevated.
labs.hint: This supports chronic alcohol-related injury but does not explain ophthalmoplegia and ataxia by itself. Avoid stopping at intoxication or liver disease.

labs.name: ECG
labs.result: Sinus tachycardia, QTc 468 ms. No ischemic changes.
labs.remark: Gerald: Is his heart in danger too?
labs.fennick: Sinus tachycardia with prolonged corrected QT; no ischaemic change.
labs.hint: The prolonged QT raises urgency around the depleted electrolytes. Which measured deficiency is both arrhythmogenic and necessary for vitamin-dependent recovery?

labs.name: VBG + lactate
labs.result: pH 7.34, bicarbonate 18, lactate 3.1 mmol/L.
labs.remark: Gerald: You can take what you need. Just help him wake up.
labs.fennick: Mild metabolic acidosis with elevated lactate.
labs.hint: Lactate reflects impaired aerobic metabolism and perfusion. Severe thiamine deficiency blocks pyruvate entry into the Krebs cycle.

labs.name: Coagulation studies
labs.result: INR 1.6.
labs.remark: Gerald: He bruises easily now. I thought it was work.
labs.fennick: The INR is prolonged.
labs.hint: This supports impaired synthesis or nutritional injury, but the neurologic emergency still rests on the bedside syndrome.

labs.name: Whole-blood thiamine
labs.result: Whole-blood thiamine is markedly below the laboratory reference interval. Result finalized several days after collection.
labs.remark: Gerald: So you were right not to wait.
labs.fennick: The concentration is markedly reduced; the result returned days after collection.
labs.hint: This confirms deficiency retrospectively. Treatment should already have started from malnutrition, ocular motor dysfunction, ataxia, and confusion.

labs.name: Ammonia
labs.result: Within the laboratory reference interval.
labs.remark: Gerald: So that liver-related toxin does not explain all of this.
labs.fennick: Ammonia is within reference range.
labs.hint: A normal ammonia weakens hepatic encephalopathy as the sole explanation and leaves the ocular motor findings and ataxia unexplained.

management.title: Immediate treatment
management.hint: Two reversible neurologic threats coexist. Thiamine should precede carbohydrate when possible, but clinically important hypoglycaemia must never be left untreated while you wait.
management.hintPatient: Gerald: He needs both treatments now, doesn’t he?
management.prompt: Suspected Wernicke encephalopathy with glucose 3.2 mmol/L. What is the safest immediate sequence?
management.promptRemark: Gerald: He is fading again. Please do something now.
management.fennick: Exactly. Give parenteral thiamine immediately, and correct glucose without avoidable delay.
management.quote: Gerald: His eyes are tracking. I think he heard me.

options.text: Give IV thiamine now, then promptly give IV dextrose
options.feedback: Correct. Give parenteral thiamine immediately before or alongside glucose, but never delay correction of clinically important hypoglycaemia while searching for thiamine. Continue thiamine after the first dose because one dose does not replenish a severe deficit.
options.patientCorrect: Gerald: You gave both. Good. He squeezed my hand.

options.text: Wait for the thiamine level before treating
options.feedback: Wernicke encephalopathy is a clinical diagnosis. Laboratory confirmation is too slow and treatment delay risks permanent neurologic injury.
options.patientWrong: Gerald: Waiting days is not a treatment plan.
options.fennWrong: A send-out level cannot safely delay a bedside diagnosis.

options.text: Give dextrose and omit thiamine because glucose is the only emergency
options.feedback: Correct hypoglycemia promptly, but omitting thiamine in this high-risk presentation leaves the underlying cerebral energy failure untreated.
options.patientWrong: Gerald: Please treat the reason this happened too.
options.fennWrong: Glucose is urgent, but omitting thiamine leaves the neurologic injury untreated.

options.text: Give oral thiamine and reassess tomorrow
options.feedback: Suspected acute Wernicke encephalopathy requires parenteral thiamine; oral absorption is unreliable and too slow here.
options.patientWrong: Gerald: Tomorrow is too late for something affecting his brain.
options.fennWrong: Oral absorption is unreliable in this acute, malnourished patient.

management.openingFenn: Two urgent deficiencies. Sequence them without delaying either.

management.title: Correct the cofactors and prevent deterioration
management.hint: Severe magnesium deficiency can blunt thiamine-dependent recovery and the prolonged QT adds electrical risk. Correct the cofactor while continuing definitive therapy and monitoring.
management.hintPatient: Gerald: The vitamin cannot work properly if another piece is missing.
management.prompt: He is more alert after thiamine and glucose. Magnesium is 0.6 mmol/L and QTc is prolonged. What is next?
management.promptRemark: Patient: This is not my restaurant. Gerald, why is this not my restaurant?
management.fennick: Replace magnesium, continue high-dose parenteral thiamine, and monitor for withdrawal and refeeding complications.
management.quote: Patient: I feel as though the room has stopped moving. Mostly.

options.text: Replace magnesium and continue IV thiamine with monitoring
options.feedback: Correct. Replace severe magnesium deficiency because it can impair thiamine-dependent recovery and prolong repolarization. Continue parenteral thiamine while monitoring rhythm, potassium, phosphate, nutrition, and withdrawal.
options.patientCorrect: Patient: Gerald, cancel breakfast service. Gerald: Already done.

options.text: Stop treatment because mental status improved
options.feedback: Early improvement does not correct severe deficiency, electrolyte abnormalities, or withdrawal risk.
options.patientWrong: Patient: Clearer is not the same as steady.
options.fennWrong: Early improvement does not replace depleted stores or correct the rhythm risk.

options.text: Repeat CT head before replacing magnesium
options.feedback: The CT is already negative. Repeating it delays treatment of a critical electrolyte abnormality without a new neurologic change.
options.patientWrong: Gerald: His scan was clear. His magnesium is not.
options.fennWrong: There is no new focal change to justify repeating a negative head scan.

options.text: Start a large carbohydrate meal immediately without electrolyte monitoring
options.feedback: Severe malnutrition creates refeeding risk. Nutrition should be introduced with electrolyte monitoring and replacement.
options.patientWrong: Patient: I would prefer dinner not create a second emergency.
options.fennWrong: A large carbohydrate load without electrolyte surveillance invites refeeding complications.

management.openingFenn: The mind is clearer; the cofactor and rhythm still need attention.

management.title: Disposition
management.hint: Persistent ataxia, parenteral treatment, electrolyte replacement, malnutrition, and possible withdrawal require observation beyond an outpatient setting.
management.hintPatient: Gerald: He is awake, but he still cannot walk safely.
management.prompt: He is improving but remains ataxic with severe nutritional and electrolyte deficiencies. Where should care continue?
management.promptRemark: Patient: I can sleep upstairs at the restaurant. Gerald can check on me.
management.fennick: This is an admission: parenteral thiamine, monitored refeeding, electrolyte replacement, and withdrawal surveillance.
management.quote: Patient: Fine. Gerald, you are in charge of the keys. Do not enjoy that sentence.

options.text: Admit for IV thiamine, refeeding, and withdrawal monitoring
options.feedback: Correct. Persistent ataxia, malnutrition, parenteral therapy, electrolyte replacement, and withdrawal risk require a monitored admission. Add nutrition and mobility assessment before discharge planning.
options.patientCorrect: Patient: One night? Fenn: Let us begin with tonight.

options.text: Discharge with oral vitamins and primary-care follow-up
options.feedback: Persistent ataxia, severe hypomagnesemia, malnutrition, and withdrawal risk require inpatient care.
options.patientWrong: Patient: Gerald would have to carry me up the restaurant stairs.
options.fennWrong: Oral vitamins cannot cover persistent ataxia, parenteral therapy, or withdrawal risk.

options.text: Transfer directly to psychiatry
options.feedback: This is an acute neurologic and metabolic emergency. Behavioral-health support follows medical stabilization.
options.patientWrong: Patient: I am ill, Doctor—not a problem to be removed from your ward.
options.fennWrong: The confusion has a medical cause that still requires active treatment.

options.text: Send him to an unmonitored detoxification facility
options.feedback: He still needs medical treatment and monitoring that a nonmedical detoxification setting cannot provide.
options.patientWrong: Gerald: He needs a hospital before he needs a program.
options.fennWrong: A nonmedical detox bed cannot replace electrolyte and neurologic monitoring.

management.openingFenn: He is improving, but he still cannot walk safely.

management.title: A useful conversation
management.hint: Begin with permission and specific medical observations. Curiosity and choice invite honesty; labels and confrontation usually close the conversation.
management.hintPatient: Gerald: Talk to him, not at him.
management.prompt: Once he is lucid, how should you begin discussing alcohol use?
management.promptRemark: Patient: I know the speech. I have heard several versions from people who were not asked.
management.fennick: Ask permission, connect the medical findings to alcohol without moral judgment, and let him choose the next step.
management.quote: Patient: You asked first. Fine. We can talk.

options.text: Ask permission, name the medical concern, and offer treatment choices
options.feedback: Correct. Permission, specific observations, and a menu of treatment choices preserve autonomy and improve engagement. Agree on one realistic next step rather than demanding a lifetime commitment at the bedside.
options.patientCorrect: Patient: Tell me what help actually looks like.

options.text: Tell him he must stop immediately or treatment will be withdrawn
options.feedback: Threats damage trust and are not an evidence-based brief intervention.
options.patientWrong: Patient: If help comes with an ultimatum, I will stop listening.
options.fennWrong: A threat turns a treatment conversation into punishment.

options.text: Avoid the subject because it may embarrass him
options.feedback: This admission is an important opportunity to offer help respectfully.
options.patientWrong: Patient: I know what we are avoiding. I would rather name it.
options.fennWrong: Avoiding the subject abandons an important prevention opportunity.

options.text: Discuss his alcohol history with Gerald without asking him
options.feedback: Once he has capacity, he controls disclosure of his medical information.
options.patientWrong: Patient: Gerald is my manager, not my medical proxy.
options.fennWrong: With capacity restored, disclosure is his choice.

management.openingFenn: Ask permission first. Then connect the illness to the exposure.

hints.fenn: Confusion plus an ocular abnormality or ataxia in a malnourished patient is enough to treat for Wernicke encephalopathy.
hints.patient: Gerald: His eyes and his balance changed before he collapsed.

hints.fenn: Do not wait for the thiamine level. This diagnosis is clinical and treatment is time-sensitive.
hints.patient: Gerald: So the result can confirm it later.

hints.fenn: Give parenteral thiamine promptly and correct hypoglycemia without avoidable delay.
hints.patient: Gerald: Both treatments. Now.

hints.fenn: Remember magnesium: severe deficiency can impair thiamine-dependent processes and increase arrhythmia risk.
hints.patient: Patient: Apparently I am deficient in several departments.

debrief.title: Wernicke Encephalopathy
debrief.pearl: Treat suspected Wernicke encephalopathy clinically with prompt parenteral thiamine. Correct hypoglycemia without avoidable delay, replace magnesium and other electrolytes, introduce nutrition carefully, and monitor for alcohol withdrawal and persistent cognitive or gait deficits.

patient.title: The Conservatory Technician
patient.occupation: Plant toxicology technician · Everfall Botanical Conservatory
patient.initialQuote: My mouth is completely dry, the room is blurring, and my heart will not slow down. I was processing belladonna samples.

fenn.initial: She has already named the exposure. Our job is to prove the physiology and keep it from escalating.
fenn.diagnosisCorrect: Good. Pure antimuscarinic poisoning fits—but treatment still begins with support and an ECG.
fenn.diagnosisWrong: Look at the skin. Similar toxidromes race the heart; only one takes the sweat away.
fenn.diagnosisUnsupported: That diagnosis cannot explain the plant exposure with dry skin, mydriasis, ileus, retention, and delirium.
fenn.differentialLocked: A dry toxidrome fits. Check conduction and mixed ingestion before considering an antidote.
fenn.debrief: She requested new glove protocols before discharge. Occupational health received a remarkably detailed memorandum.
fenn.labMenuHint: Start with an ECG and metabolic assessment. The antidote decision depends on conduction, temperature, and evidence of mixed ingestion.
fenn.labMenuPatient: The plant exposure was real. You still need to know what it did to the rest of me.

hpi: A 27-year-old conservatory technician developed blurred vision, dry mouth, palpitations, urinary retention, and confusion after processing concentrated belladonna specimens. A glove tore; she continued working and later rubbed her eyes and ate without washing. Symptoms progressed over two hours. She is frightened, hot, and intermittently loses the thread of conversation.

chart.Exposure Hx: Concentrated belladonna preparation contacted torn glove and contaminated hands; probable mucosal ingestion.
chart.Social Hx: Lives alone; no recreational drug use; workplace exposure only.

diagnosticReasoning.earlyRecognitionFeedback: Strong recognition: mydriasis, dry flushed skin, hyperthermia, tachycardia, urinary retention, ileus, and delirium form a classic antimuscarinic pattern.

mustNotMiss.feedback: Hyperthermia and altered mentation make heat stroke dangerous to miss, although the profound dryness, mydriasis, retention, and exposure point elsewhere.
Sepsis can cause fever, tachycardia, and delirium; the exposure and antimuscarinic examination argue against it.

reasonableAlternatives.feedback: Serotonin syndrome causes agitation and hyperthermia but usually includes diaphoresis, clonus, and hyperreflexia rather than dry skin and urinary retention.

finalFeedback.heat-stroke: Cooling is urgent, but the belladonna exposure plus mydriasis, anhidrosis, urinary retention, and ileus identifies an anticholinergic toxidrome.
finalFeedback.serotonin-syndrome: There is no serotonergic exposure, clonus, hyperreflexia, or diaphoresis. The patient is profoundly dry.

diagnosticReasoning.correctFeedback: Correct — anticholinergic toxidrome from belladonna alkaloid exposure. Opening management…
diagnosticReasoning.patientCorrect: That is what I thought. I would prefer being right under different circumstances.
diagnosticReasoning.patientWrong: No—I am dry. Completely dry. That difference matters.

history.title: ADDITIONAL HISTORY
history.text: A glove tore while she processed belladonna extract. She later touched her eyes and ate lunch without washing. No co-ingestants, prescribed anticholinergics, or recreational substances.
history.quote: I knew the protocol. I made one tired decision and kept working.
history.fennick: Torn glove, ocular contact, then food handling; no reported co-ingestant.
history.hint: The exposure is credible. Use the examination to distinguish a dry antimuscarinic syndrome from a sweaty sympathomimetic one.

exam.title: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
exam.text: Agitated with fluctuating attention. Pupils 8 mm and poorly reactive. Skin flushed, hot, and completely dry; mucosa dry. Sinus tachycardia. Distended bladder, absent bowel sounds, no clonus or rigidity.
exam.quote: Please turn the lights down. And please do something about my bladder.
exam.fennick: Dilated poorly reactive pupils, hot dry skin, dry mucosa, absent bowel sounds, and a distended bladder.
exam.hint: Which toxidrome combines delirium and tachycardia with anhidrosis, mydriasis, ileus, and urinary retention?

imaging.title: IMAGING
imaging.text: CT head shows no acute intracranial process. Bladder scan shows marked urinary retention.
imaging.quote: The scan is clear. The plant is still very much here.
imaging.fennick: No acute intracranial lesion; the bladder is markedly distended.
imaging.hint: The negative head study removes a competing structural emergency. Return to the exposure, skin, pupils, bowel sounds, and bladder.

labs.name: ECG
labs.result: Sinus tachycardia 128 bpm. QRS 84 ms, QTc 438 ms. No sodium-channel blockade or ventricular dysrhythmia.
labs.remark: The tracing is fast, but you said the width is normal.
labs.fennick: Sinus tachycardia; narrow QRS and no ventricular dysrhythmia.
labs.hint: A narrow QRS makes sodium-channel blockade less likely and matters before considering a centrally acting antidote.

labs.name: CMP
labs.result: Glucose 142 mg/dL; electrolytes and renal function currently preserved.
labs.remark: At least one panel is mostly boring.
labs.fennick: Mild hyperglycaemia; electrolytes and renal function preserved.
labs.hint: The metabolic panel has not supplied an alternate cause. Check conduction and complications of agitation next.

labs.name: CBC
labs.result: WBC 13.2 ×10⁹/L. Haemoglobin and platelets within reference range.
labs.remark: Stress. That seems accurate.
labs.fennick: Mild leukocytosis with normal haemoglobin and platelets.
labs.hint: Stress leukocytosis is nonspecific here. It should not distract from the exposure and dry peripheral findings.

labs.name: CK
labs.result: Creatine kinase normal initially. Repeat if hyperthermia or agitation persists.
labs.remark: So my muscles have not started breaking down.
labs.fennick: Creatine kinase is within range.
labs.hint: A normal initial CK is reassuring, but persistent hyperthermia or agitation would justify repeating it.

labs.name: VBG
labs.result: pH 7.43, pCO₂ 38, bicarbonate 25. No metabolic acidosis.
labs.remark: Good. One less emergency.
labs.fennick: Normal pH and bicarbonate; no metabolic acidosis.
labs.hint: The absence of acidosis argues against several dangerous co-ingestions but does not identify the toxidrome by itself.

labs.name: Toxicology screen
labs.result: Tropane alkaloids detected. Acetaminophen, salicylate, ethanol, and common drugs of abuse negative.
labs.remark: Only the plant. Exactly as I told you.
labs.fennick: Tropane alkaloids detected; common co-ingestants not detected.
labs.hint: Pair the detected plant alkaloid with the dry skin, mydriasis, ileus, retention, and delirium.

labs.name: Urinalysis
labs.result: Concentrated urine without pyuria or bacteriuria. Bladder scan shows marked retention.
labs.remark: I would like the catheter now, please.
labs.fennick: Concentrated urine without infection.
labs.hint: The urine does not explain the retention. The bladder finding belongs to the same autonomic pattern as the dry mouth and ileus.

labs.name: Pregnancy test
labs.result: Negative.
labs.remark: Expected, but fair to check before treatment decisions.
labs.fennick: Pregnancy test is negative.
labs.hint: This changes medication safety planning, not the leading diagnosis.

labs.name: Serum osmolality
labs.result: Serum osmolality within reference range.
labs.remark: Another quiet result. Keep going.
labs.fennick: Serum osmolality is within range.
labs.hint: No major osmolar disturbance explains the delirium. Keep the toxic exposure central.

management.title: Stabilize the toxidrome
management.hint: Before an antidote, control agitation and temperature, monitor the rhythm, secure access, and relieve retention. Supportive care is active treatment.
management.hintPatient: Please cool me down and stop my bladder from becoming another emergency.
management.prompt: She is delirious, tachycardic, hyperthermic, and retaining urine. What comes first?
management.promptRemark: The room is moving. Why is the room moving?
management.fennick: Supportive care first: monitoring, IV access, benzodiazepines, cooling, fluids as indicated, and bladder decompression.
management.quote: The lights are lower. The room is still difficult, but less hostile.

options.text: Monitor, use benzodiazepines and cooling, and drain the bladder
options.feedback: Correct. Supportive care is active treatment: monitor rhythm, secure access, use benzodiazepines for dangerous agitation, cool actively, give fluids as indicated, and decompress significant retention. Reassess temperature, CK, renal function, and airway risk.
options.patientCorrect: Thank you. I can think around the edges again.

options.text: Use haloperidol alone to control the agitation and delirium
options.feedback: Antipsychotics may worsen hyperthermia, lower seizure threshold, and complicate conduction risk. Benzodiazepines and supportive care are preferred.
options.patientWrong: The room is still burning and my bladder still hurts.
options.fennWrong: Haloperidol alone does not address heat, retention, volume status, or conduction risk.

options.text: Induce vomiting now to remove the remaining plant material
options.feedback: The exposure is already absorbed and she has ileus and delirium. Induced emesis adds aspiration risk without benefit.
options.patientWrong: Please do not make me vomit while the ceiling is moving.
options.fennWrong: With delirium and ileus, induced emesis adds aspiration without useful decontamination.

options.text: Discharge once oxygenation is confirmed normal despite the delirium
options.feedback: Normal oxygen saturation does not make delirium, hyperthermia, tachycardia, and urinary retention safe for discharge.
options.patientWrong: I cannot safely find the door, let alone go home.
options.fennWrong: Normal oxygenation does not neutralize hyperthermia, delirium, or urinary retention.

management.openingFenn: Cool her, control agitation, monitor conduction, and relieve retention.

management.title: Persistent central delirium
management.hint: The antidote is considered only after confirming a pure antimuscarinic syndrome and excluding conduction delay or a mixed sodium-channel-blocking ingestion.
management.hintPatient: You checked the tracing before considering the antidote. Good.
management.prompt: Despite supportive care, severe delirium persists. The exposure appears purely antimuscarinic and QRS is 84 ms. What is the best next step?
management.promptRemark: I know where I am. No—this is the greenhouse. Why is there a monitor in the greenhouse?
management.fennick: This is where physostigmine may help—but only with toxicology input, slow dosing, continuous monitoring, and contraindications checked.
management.quote: The greenhouse is gone. I am in a hospital. That is an improvement.

options.text: Use monitored physostigmine with toxicology input
options.feedback: Correct. In severe, confirmed pure antimuscarinic delirium with a narrow QRS, carefully titrated physostigmine may be used with toxicology support and continuous monitoring. Give it slowly with atropine and resuscitation capability available.
options.patientCorrect: Everything is suddenly much clearer. Unpleasantly clear, but clear.

options.text: Give physostigmine rapidly without ECG review
options.feedback: Physostigmine is not a reflex bolus. Exclude QRS prolongation or mixed toxicity, consult toxicology, dose slowly, and monitor for bradycardia and seizures.
options.patientWrong: That sounded much too fast for a drug meant to clear my head.
options.fennWrong: Physostigmine requires ECG review, slow dosing, monitoring, and resuscitation capability.

options.text: Give sodium bicarbonate despite a normal QRS
options.feedback: Sodium bicarbonate treats sodium-channel blockade with QRS widening; it is not indicated for isolated sinus tachycardia with QRS 84 ms.
options.patientWrong: You are treating a tracing I do not have.
options.fennWrong: Bicarbonate treats widened-QRS sodium-channel blockade, which this tracing does not show.

options.text: Give atropine to reverse the autonomic manifestations
options.feedback: Atropine is itself antimuscarinic and would worsen this toxidrome.
options.patientWrong: More dryness and confusion is not an antidote.
options.fennWrong: Atropine adds antimuscarinic activity and would intensify this syndrome.

management.openingFenn: The delirium persists. Check the tracing before choosing an antidote.

management.title: Observation and disposition
management.hint: A brief response does not guarantee sustained clearance. Think about recurrence, residual tachycardia, and the monitoring required after antidote use.
management.hintPatient: I am clearer, not necessarily finished with this.
management.prompt: Her delirium improves, but she required physostigmine and remains intermittently tachycardic. What disposition is appropriate?
management.promptRemark: I live alone. I am beginning to suspect that is relevant tonight.
management.fennick: Continue monitored observation or admission until recurrent toxicity, temperature, rhythm, cognition, and urinary function are stable.
management.quote: I will stay. Occupational health can receive my report in the morning.

options.text: Continue monitored observation until recovery remains sustained
options.feedback: Correct. Severe toxicity and physostigmine use require monitored observation for recurrent delirium, dysrhythmia, hyperthermia, and recurrent retention. Discharge only after sustained cognitive and autonomic recovery.
options.patientCorrect: A monitored bed sounds much better than being alone.

options.text: Discharge immediately after the first clear conversation
options.feedback: Physostigmine can wear off before the toxin. Recurrent delirium and peripheral toxicity must be excluded before discharge.
options.patientWrong: I am clearer, but I still do not trust myself alone tonight.
options.fennWrong: A transient lucid interval does not exclude recurrent central toxicity.

options.text: Transfer to inpatient psychiatry for hallucinations
options.feedback: The delirium is toxicologic and requires medical monitoring, not primary psychiatric admission.
options.patientWrong: The greenhouse was chemical, not psychiatric.
options.fennWrong: A psychiatric unit cannot replace post-antidote cardiac and toxicology monitoring.

options.text: Prescribe outpatient physostigmine
options.feedback: Physostigmine is an acute monitored antidote, not an outpatient prescription.
options.patientWrong: My torn glove—not an infection—started this.
options.fennWrong: Antibiotics do not treat this exposure, and there is no infectious source.

management.openingFenn: Clarity after an antidote can fade. Prove the recovery is sustained.

hints.fenn: Tachycardia and hyperthermia occur in several toxidromes. The absence of sweat is the dividing line here.
hints.patient: I cannot sweat at all.

hints.fenn: Mydriasis, dry mucosa, urinary retention, ileus, and delirium all reflect muscarinic blockade.
hints.patient: Every secretion and smooth-muscle function seems to have stopped.

hints.fenn: Before physostigmine, confirm a pure antimuscarinic syndrome and inspect the ECG—especially QRS duration.
hints.patient: The exposure was belladonna only. The tracing matters.

hints.fenn: Supportive care is not a placeholder. Cooling, benzodiazepines, monitoring, and bladder decompression are treatment.
hints.patient: The cooling helped before the antidote did.

debrief.title: Anticholinergic Toxidrome
debrief.pearl: Recognize the dry, flushed, mydriatic, tachycardic, retaining, delirious patient. Begin with supportive care and ECG assessment. Physostigmine is reserved for significant pure antimuscarinic central toxicity after contraindications are excluded and with toxicology guidance and continuous monitoring.

patient.title: The Sales Director's Cough
patient.occupation: Regional sales director · Everfall Freight Cooperative
patient.initialQuote: The cough has been there for months. The blood was new. My collar getting tighter is what finally worried my wife.

fenn.initial: He has spent months explaining each symptom away. The collar is harder to negotiate with.
fenn.diagnosisCorrect: Yes. Now separate the cancer, the obstructed vein, and the paraneoplastic findings—then manage the whole patient.
fenn.diagnosisWrong: You have named part of the picture. The histology and paraneoplastic clues demand greater specificity.
fenn.diagnosisUnsupported: That diagnosis does not connect a central hilar mass, SVC obstruction, inappropriate antidiuresis, and facilitation after exercise.
fenn.differentialLocked: A central lung malignancy fits. Establish the histology and connect the paraneoplastic findings.
fenn.debrief: He rescheduled three client meetings before telling his family. Then, finally, he let his wife take the phone.
fenn.labMenuHint: Begin with CBC, metabolic studies, and ECG. Hyponatraemia may be part of the same process, but tissue is still required.
fenn.labMenuPatient: The swelling is visible. I assume the blood work may show what else this has disturbed.

hpi: A 62-year-old regional sales director reports three months of cough, two weeks of scant hemoptysis, twelve pounds of unintentional weight loss, and six weeks of morning facial swelling. His collar is tighter and headaches worsen when bending forward. He has a 45-pack-year smoking history. He also reports proximal leg weakness that briefly improves with repeated effort.

chart.Medications: Lisinopril 10 mg daily; omeprazole 20 mg daily.
chart.Family Hx: Father died of chronic lung disease; mother had colorectal cancer.
chart.Social Hx: Regional sales travel; lives with wife; 45-pack-year smoking history; occasional alcohol.

diagnosticReasoning.earlyRecognitionFeedback: Strong recognition: central lung mass, SVC syndrome, SIADH, and Lambert-Eaton physiology strongly favor small-cell lung cancer.

mustNotMiss.feedback: This is the immediately important complication; assess for airway compromise and cerebral edema.
Lymphoma can cause a mediastinal mass and SVC syndrome and remains important until tissue diagnosis.

reasonableAlternatives.feedback: A central smoking-related mass and hemoptysis fit, but SIADH and Lambert-Eaton features point toward SCLC.
Reasonable before biopsy, but the pathology and paraneoplastic pattern support SCLC.

finalFeedback.superior-vena-cava-syndrome: Correct complication, but it does not identify the underlying malignancy. The biopsy and paraneoplastic features support SCLC.
finalFeedback.non-small-cell-lung-cancer: Lung cancer is correct broadly, but biopsy establishes small-cell histology.
finalFeedback.squamous-cell-lung-carcinoma: A central mass is compatible, but the biopsy and SIADH/Lambert-Eaton pattern favor small-cell carcinoma.

diagnosticReasoning.correctTitle: Small Cell Lung Cancer with Superior Vena Cava Syndrome
diagnosticReasoning.correctFeedback: Correct — small-cell lung cancer presenting with SVC syndrome and paraneoplastic disease. Opening management…
diagnosticReasoning.patientCorrect: Small cell. So the swelling, the sodium, and the weakness all came from the same disease.
diagnosticReasoning.patientWrong: You have explained the swelling. You have not explained the biopsy.

history.title: ADDITIONAL HISTORY
history.text: Facial swelling and headache are worse in the morning and when bending forward. He has progressive cough, hemoptysis, weight loss, 45 pack-years of smoking, and proximal weakness that improves briefly with repeated movement.
history.quote: I kept calling it travel fatigue. That explanation has expired.
history.fennick: Morning facial swelling, positional headache, cough, haemoptysis, weight loss, heavy smoking exposure, and fatigable proximal weakness.
history.hint: A central thoracic process can obstruct venous return and produce paraneoplastic neurologic findings. Which lung cancer classically does both?

exam.title: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
exam.text: Plethoric facial and bilateral arm edema, distended nonpulsatile neck veins, and chest-wall venous collaterals. Decreased right-upper-lobe breath sounds. Symmetric proximal weakness with reduced reflexes that improve after brief exercise.
exam.quote: The collar was not shrinking. I understand that now.
exam.fennick: Plethoric face, bilateral arm oedema, nonpulsatile neck veins, chest-wall collaterals, proximal weakness, and reflexes that improve after exercise.
exam.hint: The upper-body venous obstruction and facilitation after exercise point to one central malignancy with a classic presynaptic paraneoplastic syndrome.

imaging.title: IMAGING
imaging.text: Contrast CT chest shows a 6.2-cm right hilar mass compressing the SVC with mediastinal adenopathy. CT abdomen shows multiple liver lesions. Brain MRI shows no focal metastatic lesion.
imaging.quote: A mass in the chest and spots in the liver. I understand why you need tissue now.
imaging.fennick: Right hilar mass, SVC compression, mediastinal nodes, and multiple liver lesions; no focal brain lesion.
imaging.hint: A bulky central or hilar mass with SVC compression, hyponatraemia, and Lambert-Eaton physiology most strongly favors which lung cancer?

labs.name: CBC
labs.result: Hgb 10.4 g/dL with normocytic indices. Platelets 398 ×10⁹/L.
labs.remark: I expected worse.
labs.fennick: Mild normocytic anaemia; platelets preserved.
labs.hint: The anaemia is nonspecific. A metabolic panel may reveal a more characteristic paraneoplastic clue.

labs.name: CMP
labs.result: Na 128 mEq/L, serum osmolality low; renal function preserved; mild transaminitis.
labs.remark: The sodium is low because of the tumor?
labs.fennick: Hypotonic hyponatraemia with preserved renal function and mild transaminitis.
labs.hint: In a smoker with dyspnoea and a central thoracic process, hypotonic hyponatraemia should prompt evaluation for inappropriate antidiuresis.

labs.name: Urine studies
labs.result: Urine osmolality 680 mOsm/kg and urine sodium 62 mEq/L despite low serum osmolality.
labs.remark: So I am retaining water, not lacking salt.
labs.fennick: Urine remains concentrated with elevated urine sodium despite low serum osmolality.
labs.hint: Concentrated urine in hypotonic, clinically euvolaemic hyponatraemia supports inappropriate ADH activity. Which lung malignancy is most associated with it?

labs.name: ECG
labs.result: Sinus rhythm at 96 bpm. No ischemic changes or conduction abnormality.
labs.remark: One ordinary result.
labs.fennick: Sinus rhythm without ischaemic or conduction change.
labs.hint: The ECG is not the source of the upper-body swelling. Examine the venous pattern and thorax.

labs.name: VBG
labs.result: Mild hypoxemia without hypercapnia.
labs.remark: That explains the breathlessness, at least.
labs.fennick: Mild hypoxaemia without carbon-dioxide retention.
labs.hint: This confirms respiratory impairment but is not histology. Imaging is the next high-yield step.

labs.name: Bronchoscopy biopsy
labs.result: Nuclear molding, scant cytoplasm, high mitotic rate, synaptophysin/chromogranin/CD56 positive, Ki-67 >80%.
labs.remark: Those cells are answering the question the scan could not.
labs.fennick: Nuclear molding, scant cytoplasm, brisk mitoses, neuroendocrine markers, and a very high proliferation index.
labs.hint: This combination describes a high-grade neuroendocrine lung carcinoma. Name the specific diagnosis.

labs.name: Pulmonary function
labs.result: Mild obstructive ventilatory defect.
labs.remark: Years of smoking left more than one mark.
labs.fennick: Mild obstructive physiology.
labs.hint: The obstruction reflects smoking injury but cannot explain venous collaterals, liver lesions, or the central mass.

labs.name: EMG
labs.result: Incremental compound motor response with high-frequency repetitive nerve stimulation.
labs.remark: The weakness was connected too.
labs.fennick: High-frequency stimulation produces an incremental motor response.
labs.hint: Facilitation suggests a presynaptic neuromuscular-junction syndrome strongly associated with one lung cancer subtype.

labs.name: LDH
labs.result: LDH elevated above reference range.
labs.remark: Another sign that something is moving quickly.
labs.fennick: LDH is elevated.
labs.hint: Elevated LDH is nonspecific but compatible with a high-burden, rapidly proliferative process.

management.title: Assess the SVC syndrome
management.hint: First decide whether the obstruction is immediately threatening the airway or brain. Without those red flags, stabilize, coordinate specialists, and preserve the chance for a useful tissue diagnosis.
management.hintPatient: The swelling is frightening, but I can still breathe and think clearly.
management.prompt: He has facial edema and headache but no stridor, airway compromise, syncope, or cerebral edema. What is the best immediate plan?
management.promptRemark: My face is worse when I lean forward, but I can breathe.
management.fennick: Elevate him, monitor closely, and expedite tissue diagnosis and multidisciplinary treatment. Reserve emergent stenting for life-threatening obstruction.
management.quote: Good. A plan based on severity, not panic.

options.text: Elevate the head, monitor closely, and expedite tissue diagnosis
options.feedback: Correct. Without stridor, cerebral oedema, syncope, or airway compromise, elevate the head, monitor closely, and expedite tissue diagnosis with pulmonology and oncology. Escalate to urgent endovascular or radiation intervention if life-threatening features develop.
options.patientCorrect: You are moving quickly without pretending every procedure is an emergency.

options.text: Start anticoagulation for presumed thrombosis
options.feedback: CT shows tumor compression without documented thrombosis. Anticoagulation is not treatment for pure extrinsic obstruction and hemoptysis increases bleeding concern.
options.patientWrong: I am coughing blood already. Do not add bleeding risk without a clot.
options.fennWrong: There is no documented thrombus; anticoagulation does not relieve pure external compression.

options.text: Use aggressive diuresis to reduce upper-body venous congestion
options.feedback: Diuresis does not relieve the obstruction and may cause dehydration. It is not definitive treatment.
options.patientWrong: Less fluid will not move the mass off the vein.
options.fennWrong: Diuresis cannot open a vein compressed by a hilar mass.

options.text: Place an emergent SVC stent before assessing severity or obtaining tissue
options.feedback: Endovascular stenting is valuable for severe or life-threatening symptoms, but routine immediate stenting is not required in this stable presentation.
options.patientWrong: I want urgency, not a procedure chosen before the severity is judged.
options.fennWrong: Without airway or cerebral compromise, immediate stenting before tissue is not automatically required.

management.openingFenn: First grade the SVC obstruction: airway and neurologic danger change the urgency.

management.title: Confirm and stage before definitive therapy
management.hint: Imaging can show where disease is; tissue shows what it is. Treatment direction needs both histology and staging, including the brain.
management.hintPatient: You need to know both the type and how far it has travelled.
management.prompt: What investigation establishes treatment direction?
management.promptRemark: If this is cancer, I would like the exact kind before anyone treats it.
management.fennick: Tissue first, then complete staging. SCLC can mimic other thoracic malignancies and stage changes the plan.
management.quote: The biopsy has a name. Small cell.

options.text: Obtain tissue and complete systemic and brain staging
options.feedback: Correct. Obtain tissue and complete systemic and brain staging before definitive therapy. Imaging defines distribution; histology determines the treatment pathway.
options.patientCorrect: Specific, staged, and not guessed. Good.

options.text: Classify and treat the tumor from its CT appearance alone
options.feedback: Imaging cannot reliably distinguish SCLC from NSCLC or lymphoma. Tissue confirmation is required unless an immediate life-threatening intervention cannot wait.
options.patientWrong: I asked for the exact kind, not the shape on a scan.
options.fennWrong: CT cannot reliably separate the possible thoracic histologies.

options.text: Proceed directly to surgical resection with nodal dissection
options.feedback: A bulky central mass with mediastinal nodes and liver metastases is not a surgical presentation.
options.patientWrong: Removing one piece would leave the rest behind.
options.fennWrong: A central mass with nodal and liver disease is not an upfront surgical presentation.

options.text: Follow serial chest radiographs before deciding on tissue sampling
options.feedback: Serial plain films delay histologic diagnosis and staging.
options.patientWrong: Watching the shadow grow is not a diagnostic plan.
options.fennWrong: Serial radiographs postpone the tissue diagnosis without answering it.

management.openingFenn: Imaging maps the disease. Tissue determines what it is.

management.title: Treat extensive-stage SCLC
management.hint: This is systemic, rapidly proliferative disease. Build the first-line regimen from a platinum backbone, a topoisomerase inhibitor, and immune checkpoint therapy.
management.hintPatient: One drug will not be the whole plan, will it?
management.prompt: Biopsy confirms SCLC and liver metastases establish extensive-stage disease. What is standard first-line systemic treatment?
management.promptRemark: Tell me the treatment that addresses all of it, not only the chest.
management.fennick: Platinum-etoposide plus a PD-L1 inhibitor is the modern systemic backbone for eligible patients.
management.quote: Systemic treatment. That matches a systemic disease.

options.text: Use platinum-etoposide plus a PD-L1 inhibitor
options.feedback: Correct. Eligible patients with extensive-stage disease receive platinum-etoposide plus a PD-L1 inhibitor, followed by maintenance immunotherapy. Treatment planning should also address symptoms, performance status, and goals of care.
options.patientCorrect: I will need the schedule in writing. My wife will insist.

options.text: Use lobectomy with nodal dissection as definitive treatment
options.feedback: Extensive-stage SCLC is systemic and not managed with resection of the primary mass alone.
options.patientWrong: The liver findings would still be there after lung surgery.
options.fennWrong: Local resection cannot treat extensive systemic disease.

options.text: Begin EGFR-inhibitor monotherapy from the imaging pattern
options.feedback: EGFR-directed therapy is for selected NSCLC, not standard SCLC treatment.
options.patientWrong: That sounds precise for somebody else’s cancer.
options.fennWrong: EGFR monotherapy targets selected non-small-cell tumors, not this histology.

options.text: Use symptom-directed observation with interval restaging
options.feedback: SCLC is aggressive but initially treatment-responsive. Delay permits rapid progression.
options.patientWrong: I did not clear my calendar so we could wait for this to worsen.
options.fennWrong: This tumor can progress rapidly; observation sacrifices a treatment-responsive window.

management.openingFenn: This is systemic, fast-growing disease; choose a systemic first-line regimen.

management.title: Manage mild SIADH
management.hint: The sodium is low but there are no severe neurologic symptoms. Correct the driver, restrict free water, and monitor rather than reaching immediately for hypertonic rescue.
management.hintPatient: No seizure, no coma—so correct it carefully.
management.prompt: Sodium is 128 without seizure or severe neurologic symptoms. What is appropriate?
management.promptRemark: The sodium is low, but I am thinking clearly.
management.fennick: Restrict free water, monitor sodium carefully, review medications, and treat the underlying SCLC.
management.quote: Less water, regular checks, and treatment of the cause. Understood.

options.text: Fluid restriction with serial sodium monitoring while treating the malignancy
options.feedback: Correct. Mild, minimally symptomatic SIADH is managed with fluid restriction, serial sodium checks, and treatment of the malignancy. Severe neurologic symptoms require carefully monitored hypertonic saline; selected refractory cases may need specialist-guided second-line therapy.
options.patientCorrect: I can follow a limit if someone gives me an actual number.

options.text: Rapidly normalize sodium with repeated 3% saline boluses
options.feedback: Hypertonic saline is reserved for severe neurologic symptoms. Overcorrection risks osmotic demyelination.
options.patientWrong: I am thinking clearly. Please do not correct this faster than is safe.
options.fennWrong: Hypertonic saline is rescue therapy for severe neurologic symptoms, not routine rapid normalization.

options.text: Give a large normal-saline bolus as definitive SIADH treatment
options.feedback: Isotonic saline may fail or worsen hyponatremia when urine remains concentrated. Address free water and the cause.
options.patientWrong: A large bag of saline sounds simpler than the problem is.
options.fennWrong: Isotonic saline may not correct SIADH while urine remains concentrated.

options.text: Ignore the sodium because cancer treatment will eventually fix it
options.feedback: The underlying cancer must be treated, but sodium still requires monitoring and interim management.
options.patientWrong: Eventually is not a monitoring schedule.
options.fennWrong: Cancer treatment addresses the driver, but the sodium still needs an interim plan and surveillance.

management.openingFenn: The sodium is low without severe neurologic symptoms. Correct it carefully.

hints.fenn: Facial and arm edema, nonpulsatile neck veins, and chest-wall collaterals identify SVC obstruction.
hints.patient: My collar is the clue you can see.

hints.fenn: A central mass in a heavy smoker narrows the field; SIADH and Lambert-Eaton narrow it further.
hints.patient: The sodium and weakness were not separate problems.

hints.fenn: The scan stages the disease, but tissue determines the histology.
hints.patient: You need the biopsy before the treatment name.

hints.fenn: For extensive-stage SCLC, think platinum-etoposide plus PD-L1 inhibition.
hints.patient: A systemic treatment for a systemic disease.

debrief.title: Small Cell Lung Cancer with SVC Syndrome
debrief.pearl: SCLC may present through local compression and paraneoplastic syndromes. Assess SVC syndrome severity first, obtain tissue promptly when the airway and brain are not threatened, stage accurately, and treat extensive-stage disease with platinum-etoposide plus immunotherapy when appropriate.

patient.title: The Councilor's Prescription
patient.initialQuote: My tailor noticed the change first. Weight here, bruises everywhere, and stairs have become surprisingly political.

fenn.initial: He arrived with a schedule and half a medication list. The missing half is usually where the case lives.
fenn.diagnosisCorrect: Exactly. This is iatrogenic Cushing syndrome; the medication history is the diagnostic test.
fenn.diagnosisWrong: The phenotype is real, but before searching for a tumor, ask what cortisol-like substance he already takes.
fenn.diagnosisUnsupported: That diagnosis cannot explain the glucocorticoid phenotype plus eighteen months of daily prednisone. Start with the medication exposure.
fenn.differentialLocked: Glucocorticoid excess fits. Determine whether its source is prescribed or endogenous before scanning glands.
fenn.debrief: He requested the taper in calendar format. Fenn supplied one with fewer committee meetings than expected.
fenn.labMenuHint: Check metabolic, cardiovascular, and bone complications first. Hormonal interpretation is distorted while supraphysiologic prednisone continues.
fenn.labMenuPatient: If the tablets caused this, show me what else they have changed.

hpi: A 40-year-old city councilor reports eighteen months of progressive central weight gain, facial rounding, easy bruising, proximal weakness, irritability, and worsening hypertension. He initially lists only amlodipine. When specifically asked about injections, creams, supplements, and medications from other prescribers, he reveals prednisone 20 mg daily for eighteen months for back pain.

chart.Medications: Amlodipine 10 mg daily. Prednisone 20 mg daily from an outside prescriber for 18 months.
chart.Social Hx: City councilor; married; no tobacco; drinks socially.

diagnosticReasoning.earlyRecognitionFeedback: Strong recognition: the Cushing phenotype plus prolonged supraphysiologic prednisone establishes an exogenous cause.

mustNotMiss.feedback: Not the current diagnosis, but abrupt glucocorticoid cessation after prolonged therapy could precipitate adrenal crisis.

reasonableAlternatives.feedback: Pituitary Cushing disease causes endogenous hypercortisolism, but the medication history provides a more direct exogenous cause.
Weight gain can suggest hypothyroidism, but wide purple striae, thin skin, bruising, and proximal weakness favor glucocorticoid excess.
Metabolic syndrome can explain central adiposity and hypertension, but not the full catabolic skin and muscle phenotype.

finalFeedback.cushing-disease-pituitary-acth-secreting: The phenotype is Cushing syndrome, but long-term prednisone makes this iatrogenic rather than pituitary disease.
finalFeedback.hypothyroidism: Hypothyroidism does not explain the wide purple striae, skin fragility, and prolonged prednisone exposure.
finalFeedback.metabolic-syndrome: Metabolic syndrome is incomplete; chronic glucocorticoid exposure unifies the findings.

diagnosticReasoning.correctTitle: Iatrogenic Cushing Syndrome from Chronic Prednisone
diagnosticReasoning.correctFeedback: Correct — iatrogenic Cushing syndrome. The next challenge is reducing glucocorticoid exposure safely.
diagnosticReasoning.patientCorrect: The prescription caused this. I would like to stop it—but I assume you are about to tell me not tonight.
diagnosticReasoning.patientWrong: Before you order a scan, should we discuss the prednisone I have taken every morning for eighteen months?

history.title: ADDITIONAL HISTORY
history.text: Targeted medication reconciliation reveals prednisone 20 mg every morning for 18 months, repeatedly renewed for lumbar radicular pain. No recent review, inhaled steroid, injection, or topical high-potency steroid.
history.quote: It controlled the pain, so I kept renewing it. Nobody connected it to the rest of this.
history.fennick: Prednisone every morning for eighteen months, repeatedly renewed without review; no other major glucocorticoid exposure.
history.hint: Before searching for an endogenous cortisol source, identify the cortisol-like medication already present and its duration.

exam.title: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
exam.text: Moon facies, dorsocervical and supraclavicular fat pads, central adiposity, thin extremities, wide violaceous striae, easy bruising, skin fragility, and proximal muscle weakness. No acute infection or heart failure.
exam.quote: The bruises appear after handshakes. That has become inconvenient professionally.
exam.fennick: Facial and truncal adiposity, violaceous striae, skin fragility, bruising, thin extremities, and proximal weakness.
exam.hint: These are glucocorticoid effects. Decide whether the source is endogenous or already listed in the medication history.

imaging.title: IMAGING
imaging.text: Lumbar MRI shows degenerative disease without cord compression, destructive lesion, or another surgical emergency.
imaging.quote: Another scan, and it found the same worn back everyone already knew about.
imaging.fennick: Degenerative lumbar change; no cord compression or surgical lesion.
imaging.hint: This scan explains neither the systemic phenotype nor the prolonged glucocorticoid exposure. Return to medication reconciliation.

labs.name: CMP
labs.result: K 3.1 mEq/L, fasting glucose 128 mg/dL; renal and liver function preserved.
labs.remark: The potassium and glucose both need follow-up.
labs.fennick: Hypokalaemia and elevated fasting glucose; renal and liver function preserved.
labs.hint: These are metabolic complications of glucocorticoid excess, but they do not locate the source.

labs.name: HbA1c
labs.result: HbA1c 6.4%.
labs.remark: Not quite over the line, but not reassuring either.
labs.fennick: Glycated haemoglobin is elevated below the diabetes threshold.
labs.hint: Chronic glucocorticoid exposure can worsen glycaemia. Treat the risk while addressing the exposure.

labs.name: CBC
labs.result: Neutrophilic leukocytosis; no fever or localizing infectious symptoms.
labs.remark: An abnormal count without an infection.
labs.fennick: Neutrophilic leukocytosis without an infectious pattern.
labs.hint: Glucocorticoids can demarginate neutrophils. The count alone should not trigger an infection diagnosis.

labs.name: Lipid panel
labs.result: LDL and triglycerides are above reference range.
labs.remark: Another item for the agenda.
labs.fennick: LDL and triglycerides are elevated.
labs.hint: This adds cardiovascular risk and belongs in follow-up, not in source localization.

labs.name: DEXA scan
labs.result: Low bone mineral density for age; no fragility fracture identified.
labs.remark: The back medication weakened the bones. That is difficult to appreciate.
labs.fennick: Bone density is low for age; no fragility fracture.
labs.hint: Long-term systemic glucocorticoids accelerate bone loss. Prevention and treatment cannot wait for the taper to finish.

labs.name: ECG
labs.result: Sinus rhythm with voltage criteria for LVH.
labs.remark: The blood pressure has been leaving a record.
labs.fennick: Sinus rhythm with voltage criteria for left-ventricular hypertrophy.
labs.hint: The tracing reflects chronic pressure burden rather than an endocrine source.

labs.name: Morning cortisol and ACTH
labs.result: Morning cortisol and ACTH are suppressed while the patient is taking supraphysiologic prednisone.
